name: Daria Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for an employer, AI company, union, political party or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. What is a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Daria, 27, and I lead a little electrical crew doing homes and shop repairs. I've got a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence; I worked hard for both, but our small firm still pays below what this trade can earn. Yesterday I traced a fault behind a bakery freezer, then spent the afternoon checking two younger workers' testing sheets. Finding the actual fault is satisfying; chasing permission to buy parts wears me down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What are work and money like away from that satisfying bit?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm single, renting a small flat, with no children and about three weeks of bills saved. There are few other electrical employers close enough for the early starts, so being good at this doesn't mean I can walk into better pay. I use AI occasionally to tidy a customer note after a colleague has tried the tool first, never to decide whether a circuit is safe. I like changes that can show me a result, rather than a promise.

say: I'd welcome **quieter change** and let the office save small amounts of time on invoices.
I want the crew to finish **repairs properly** without constant announcements about new machines.
think: My **three-week cushion** leaves me worried even if hands-on electrical work carries on as usual.
My responsibility and licence don't fix **low pay** or create other electrical employers nearby.
do: Keep the usual **repair rota** through the plateau's first year.
Redirect one weekly takeaway's cost into **savings**, aiming for another week's bills if paid hours hold.
feel: **Anxious** about a late wage payment, rather than about AI taking the electrical work.
S0.quote: My master electrician's licence doesn't pay the rent between wage days.
fieldNote: Her **anxiety** predates the scenario and comes from a short financial cushion despite skilled, responsible work.
She treats **small savings** as a limited buffer and won't threaten resignation without another actual offer.

steps.text: Keep leading the usual home and shop repair rota
Save one weekly takeaway's cost while paid hours hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that a quieter technology story would suit me. Let the office save ten minutes on an invoice and let us finish the repairs properly. I don't need a machine announcement every time I order a switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My worry would still be the gap between being responsible for a crew and having three weeks of money. Routine office savings wouldn't remove the need for my hands, but a late wage payment would still hurt. My master electrician's licence doesn't pay the rent between wage days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this month I'd keep the crew's usual repair rota and move one small takeaway meal a week into my savings account instead. If the plateau became clear, I'd keep doing that through the first year rather than buy another tool on credit. I'd aim to add one week's basic bills by the year's end, if my paid hours held.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about ordinary life, honestly, rather than frightened of AI. I can sleep when the wages arrive, and start checking the banking app when they're a day late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill or purchase would you change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent comes first, then power and the bus pass for getting to the yard. I'd drop the takeaway before any of those. I'm not pretending that makes a large safety fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you challenge your pay if the job itself stayed steady?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the owner to sit down with my responsibilities and pay, but I wouldn't threaten to leave without an offer. There aren't many nearby firms to ask. I want an agreement I can live with, not a dramatic walkout.

say: I'd judge the **booking system** by whether it leaves real time for repairs and checked customer messages.
I wouldn't promise the crew **job security** just because robots spread slowly.
think: My **hands-on work** still needs doing, but faster quotes could bring tighter schedules and less paid planning.
I could lose **income** before any robot starts pulling cable in a customer's kitchen.
do: Learn the proven **quoting assistant** with a colleague and compare its parts lists weekly during the first year.
Record **paid hours** and ask the owner to agree payment for planning before accepting more stops.
feel: **Anxious** about fewer paid hours, while willing to learn a tool that proves useful.
S1.quote: I could lose hours even while my tool bag stays busy.
fieldNote: She separates **physical demand** for electrical repairs from the employer's ability to compress paid time around each visit.
Her **tool trial** is cautious and checked; further job enquiries depend on evidence of lower wages.

steps.text: Compare the proven quoting assistant with personal parts lists every Friday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should check whether the new booking system actually leaves more time for repairs. I'm happy to lose the copying from job sheets, provided someone checks what reaches the customer. I wouldn't tell the crew that slower robots mean nobody has a problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my day is still pulling cable, testing and explaining faults in someone's kitchen. But if the office prices jobs faster, the owner might pack more stops into the same day or cut our paid planning time. I could lose hours even while my tool bag stays busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask a colleague to show me the quoting assistant that already works for them, using old job details without customer names. During the first year I'd spend half an hour each Friday comparing its parts list with my own for that week's repairs. I'd also keep a paper record of paid hours and raise any missing planning time with the owner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, with a sharper edge than the plateau. I can deal with learning a proven tool; I can't cover fewer paid hours by feeling cheerful about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop trusting the quoting assistant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check cable sizes and protective devices against our normal rules, not against a fluent answer. If an answer was wrong, I'd mark the example and stop using that part of the assistant. My licence is attached to my work, not to the software's confidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the owner added stops without paying for planning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the owner four weeks of job time, including the planning and customer explanations. I'd ask what is paid before accepting a fuller schedule. If the answer meant lower wages, I'd start asking those few nearby firms about actual vacancies.

say: I'd separate **2028 desk changes** from the hands-on robot competition expected around 2031 in this picture.
I'd ask for **dates and numbers** before accepting reassurance about what happens to our crew.
think: I could keep doing **repairs** yet lose enough checking and planning pay to struggle with rent.
The **robot gap** gives me time to look for work, without guaranteeing the wages I need.
do: Postpone the **phone replacement** now and keep the money for bills.
Ask my sister about conditional **temporary housing** and its costs before giving notice on my flat.
Apply for reachable posted **maintenance vacancies** during 2028's first year, comparing written hours and travel costs.
feel: **Anxious**, with practical options, but uncomfortable about having to ask family for a possible bed.
S2.quote: The three-year robot gap buys work time, not a promise about my wages.
fieldNote: Her **housing contingency** is a request, not assured family support, and she would establish limits before relying on it.
She sees **maintenance vacancies** as a possible immediate improvement rather than permanent protection from the stated endpoint.

steps.text: Postpone replacing the old phone and retain the money for bills
Ask the sister about three months of housing if wages fall
Apply for reachable posted maintenance jobs after checking written paid hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that AGI by 2028 isn't the same as a robot arriving tomorrow. Quotes and schedules could change in 2028; the hands-on competition in this picture comes around 2031. I'd ask for dates and numbers before anyone told us to relax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years feels short when spare cash comes in tiny pieces. I think we'd still have repair calls after 2028, but I could see my paid checking and planning hours shrinking enough to hit the rent. The three-year robot gap buys work time, not a promise about my wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd put off replacing my old phone and keep that money for bills. I'd speak to my sister about staying in her spare room if my rent became impossible. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for posted electrical maintenance vacancies I could reach, checking the actual paid hours before leaving this crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious enough that I'd calculate the rent twice, but I wouldn't say I had no plan. I still have practical skill to sell during the robot gap. Asking my sister for a possible bed would be the hard conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would you ask your sister?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my sister I wasn't asking her to promise unlimited housing. I'd ask whether three months could be possible if my hours fell, and what I should pay towards bills. She might say no, and I'd need to know that before giving notice on my flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a maintenance vacancy worth taking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the written hours and travel costs with this wage first. A maintenance title isn't proof that AGI can't touch the planning or that later robots won't touch the repairs. I'd want a better immediate footing, not a story about being safe forever.

say: I'd use **five years** to check changes before copying them across our electrical repair work.
I'd still ask how **faster planning** affects paid time, even with robots pushed back to about 2034.
think: I have time to improve my **cash buffer** while practical repair work still looks useful nearby.
I expect my **wage** to hold over the next few years if repair orders remain steady.
do: Continue the small **saving plan** while paid hours hold.
Take the **diagnosis refresher** before 2031 only with employer-paid fees and protected work hours.
Use checked **diagnostic tools** after 2031 and compare paid hours each month.
feel: **Anxious** about today's thin cash buffer, though less pressed by AI's timing than in the fast picture.
S3.quote: I can want training and still refuse a bill I can't cover.
fieldNote: Her **conditional course** depends on both fee funding and maintained working hours, rather than willingness alone.
She expects **repair wages** to hold if orders remain steady, yet a late payment still threatens today's thin buffer.

steps.text: Save one weekly takeaway's cost while paid hours hold
Take fault-diagnosis training only with employer funding and protected work hours
Use checked diagnostic AI on repairs after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us space to check each change before copying it. I'd still want the owner to show how a faster office changes our paid time. The robot date moving to about 2034 doesn't excuse treating planning as free now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with 2028, I have a chance to get more than three weeks of bills behind me. My repair work looks useful for the next few years, although wages and future robot competition still worry me. I wouldn't leave a skilled job today just because the end date has a name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd keep putting the takeaway money aside while paid hours held. Before 2031 I'd take the trade association's evening fault-diagnosis refresher if the employer paid the fee and kept my working hours intact. In the first year after 2031 I'd use the checked diagnostic tools on repairs and keep comparing the paid hours every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious about a late wage because I only have three weeks of bills saved today. Five years would give me more room to improve that, but the calendar doesn't put money into my account now. The extra time means I can ask for a sensible course arrangement rather than grab the first advertisement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the employer refused the course fee or protected work hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I wouldn't book the course on credit. I'd carry on with the small saving plan and ask again at the next work review. I can want training and still refuse a bill I can't cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the extra years feel useful in real life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to see our actual hours staying paid over several months, not one reassuring meeting. I'd also want the savings balance to stop falling whenever a bill lands. Until then, extra years would help without making me carefree.

say: I'd tell younger workers to learn **electrical work** properly during the decade instead of waiting for demonstrations.
I'd use the time for **ordinary decisions** rather than claim a safe career has already been found.
think: At **37 in 2036**, I'd still face a long career after thinking AI and later hands-on robots arrive.
I expect the present **repair wage** to continue while I build choices over a much longer preparation period.
do: Continue small **savings transfers** and review annually whether wages allow a larger amount.
Take the proven **refresher** before 2036 only with employer-paid fees and protected work hours.
Review terms after 2036 and apply for posted **repair jobs** only when written terms improve.
feel: **Anxious** about the current rent buffer, but less cornered by the longer preparation period.
S4.quote: The first target is still a buffer that lasts longer than one late payslip.
fieldNote: She refuses to count **future household assets** or a possible partner's income as resources she already has.
Her **longer preparation** remains a series of paid-work and savings decisions, not a claim that repair skills last forever.

steps.text: Review the small savings transfer annually against actual wages
Take the refresher only with employer funding and protected work hours
Apply after 2036 for posted repair jobs offering better written terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the younger workers we should learn the trade properly during that decade, not wait for a robot demonstration. I'd say the same to myself, actually. Ten years is enough to make several ordinary decisions well, if the pay lets you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 37 when the thinking work changes fully, not at the end of working life. The hands-on competition around 2039 would still leave most of my career ahead. But right now I'd expect the repair wage to continue, and I'd have much longer to build choices around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd make the same small saving transfer, with a yearly check on whether I could raise it. Before 2036 I'd repeat that proven, employer-funded refresher arrangement rather than buy an expensive promise of a safe career. In the first year after 2036 I'd review paid hours and apply for a posted repair job elsewhere only if the written terms were better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious when I picture next month's rent and only three weeks of bills saved. The decade lets me think beyond that pressure, without removing it today. I wouldn't feel happy about robots becoming so capable around 2039, but I could watch the real work change before deciding where to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the longer timeline change your plans for a home or family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, that's years away and depends on wages and housing costs I don't know yet. I wouldn't count a partner's money or an imagined house as my safety plan. The first target is still a buffer that lasts longer than one late payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you avoid putting every decision off for ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a yearly note of our pay, open jobs and what machines can actually do on older houses. If better written terms appeared, I'd apply; otherwise I'd stay and keep checking. I wouldn't set a moving date today for a place I haven't found.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I'd have so little time to turn this skill into a financial cushion. Written paid hours and a course paid for without cutting my wages would help more than a cheerful presentation. Being trusted with dangerous work and being paid enough to sleep should come together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask who pays for the time between jobs when a system books a day. Travel, checking and explaining things to a frightened customer are work too. I don't want those minutes to disappear just because a screen doesn't show them.

headlineQuote: Being trusted with dangerous work and being paid enough to sleep should come together.
portrait: **Daria, 27**, leads electrical repairs with a technical diploma and master licence, while earning low pay in a limited local market.
Single and childless, she has only **three weeks** of bills saved and uses AI occasionally after others prove its worth.
Her **practical approach** tests tools and written pay terms; fast change threatens income before robots can replace hands-on work.
Longer timelines permit **conditional training** and small savings, without assuming future assets or a permanently protected trade.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves too little time to turn her electrical skill into a financial cushion.
whatWouldHelp: **Written paid hours** would make planning possible.
Employer-funded training with **maintained wages** would help without creating another bill.
